sections.label: 1 - SORT AI FROM AUTOMATION
sections.note: Before anything gets ranked, every manual pile gets one question asked of it: does a human make a judgement call here, or is someone just moving data from one place to another. Trade logs out of Excel into a real database, lead lists, the email tool nobody trusts, the marketing side - that is plain automation on AWS, no model involved. Only what needs judgement goes into the AI lane.

sections.label: 2 - TICKETS FIRST, CHEAPEST WIN
sections.note: Support tickets are the cheapest real AI win you have, and the safest place to start. Ninety days of tickets cluster into a short list of repeat questions, and an assistant grounded in your own docs answers those and hands everything else to a person. This is not a scripted FAQ bot - it reads the question and cites your documentation - but it is also not a research project.

sections.label: 3 - ID CHECKS SECOND
sections.note: 120 ID checks a week done by eye is the next thing to shrink. Document OCR pulls the fields off the upload and a face match scores the selfie against the ID photo. This is a vendor API, not a model you train. Clear scores decide themselves and get logged, and the ambiguous ones still reach a human - just far fewer of them.

sections.label: 4 - ANOMALY DETECTION, RULES BEFORE NEURAL NETS
sections.note: The most urgent item is the one to build last, and honestly. Statistical rules on trade velocity, size and z-scores catch a surprising share of suspicious patterns, and they are explainable when someone asks why an account got flagged. Measure them against what your humans catch before spending a dollar on a model. If the rules genuinely miss real cases, the next step is a scikit-learn model on your dataset, not TensorFlow and not deep learning.

sections.label: 5 - WHAT YOU WALK AWAY WITH
sections.note: One page at the end of the hour: the four areas in build order, an effort range on each, which AWS pieces they need, and a plain column marking what is genuinely AI and what is just automation someone has been calling AI. The blockchain project is accounted for in the data work. You can hand that page to whoever you hire next.

input_sample.business: small cryptocurrency trading tool, plus a separate blockchain project
input_sample.trade_log: Microsoft Excel, about 40,000 rows, updated by hand
input_sample.support_tickets: about 300 a month, answered from scratch every time
input_sample.identity_checks: about 120 a week, ID and selfie approved by eye
input_sample.lead_lists: spreadsheets updated by hand, email tool nobody trusts
input_sample.stack: everything on AWS, React and Node.js dashboard
input_sample.assumption_on_the_table: Python and TensorFlow for anomaly detection

output_sample.rank_1_support_tickets: AI, real - top 10 questions answered from your docs, 1 to 2 weeks, deflects roughly half of 300 a month
output_sample.rank_2_identity_checks: AI via vendor API, not a model you train - OCR plus face match, 2 to 3 weeks, most of 120 a week decide themselves
output_sample.rank_3_anomaly_rules: not AI yet - statistical rules on velocity, size and z-scores, 2 to 3 weeks, measured against your humans before any model
output_sample.rank_3b_anomaly_model: only if the rules miss real cases - scikit-learn isolation forest on 40,000 rows, 3 to 4 weeks, a data scientist joins if a neural net is ever justified
output_sample.rank_4_growth: plain automation - Excel to a database, lead lists and email sequences on AWS, 1 to 2 weeks per piece
output_sample.honest_split: 2 of 4 areas are genuinely AI today, the rest is automation being called AI
output_sample.tensorflow_verdict: wrong tool at your dataset size - scikit-learn first, deep learning is not justified yet
output_sample.deliverable: one page you can hand to whoever you hire next
